utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you, too. You may be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and also good afternoon to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I am here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our acting case manager, Ms. Sanja Bokulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to our colleagues from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and I appear on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. Together with me there are Ms. Adisa Mehic, our legal assistant, and Mr. Geoff Roberts, our CaseMap manager. Mr. Jones, due to his obligations and his duties in London will not be present today but he will return shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Vidovic. Let us deal -- first of all, do you have any preliminaries yourself, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday we filed a reply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Reply in the third-party request for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Nikolic one --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- access to information. It was on close of business, and I refer to that filing. I trust the Defence already received a copy. We also would like to oppose the 92 bis motion in written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when are we going to expect that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. We should be able to provide by the end of the week. It might be Monday, but I trust we will be fine again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want you to understand, both of you, please, that as we plod ahead and approach the end of this trial, every day counts. So if you are going to oppose the application of Rule 92 bis testimony for these two witnesses, and for the -- for argument's sake let's say we agree with you, then they have to make arrangements to bring these two persons. So -- which brings me, actually, to two other things. I mean -- please remain standing because I will deal with them straight away. I am informed by my Legal Officer that in relation to the Defence response to decision on urgent Defence motion regarding prosecutorial non-compliance with Rule 68 filed on the 17th of November, and Defence response to Prosecution declaration searches, stating searches, et cetera, that you ask to have 14 days within which to reply to the first one, the tick one, in other words, with the various documents; and seven days to reply to the second. Now, I will not waste too much words on this last one, because the seven days will lapse on Thursday in any case, and today is Tuesday, so at the end of the day we are talking of just two days more and that's it, finished. I do recognise that this might require a few days more, but not 14 days. I mean, why ask for the pound of flesh when we are so tight for time and when we are trying to economise as much as possible on time and I am putting pressure on both of you to economise on time. And the end result could entail a further delay in the proceedings, because we will have to deal with all this. I mean, I anticipate that we will have to spend -- and again, half a sitting on new allegations of -- a new allegation of non-observance of Rule 68 -- 68. As you know, there is one allegation -- one fresh allegation with a forewarning of more to come. I mean, please do try to understand the concerns, the preoccupation, that we have. So I am not going to give you 14 days, but I am not going to give you much less. You will have until Monday, yesterday week in other words. The date would be the 28th of November to respond -- respond to this. And Thursday is okay for the other one. But please don't put us in a position where we have to pressurise you even further because we need to move on. We need to move on, and this is frightening. The way things are going, it's frightening. So the position, Madam Registrar, is as follows: That with regard to the Prosecution request to be able to respond to the Defence response to Prosecution declaration stating searches, location of searches, et cetera, filed on the 17th of November, the Prosecution will have until the end of the day for registry purposes of Thursday, Thursday -- this Thursday. As regards the other one, the Prosecution's request to respond to the Defence response to decision on urgent Defence motion regarding prosecutorial non-compliance with Rule 68, our preference would be if you could file it by the end of Friday, so that we can take it home with us, read it, study it, and on Monday we can come back fully cognizant of what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you make an effort, I am sure you can file all this by the end of business on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I haven't -- I have made a request to do for making use for 14 days, rather I confirmed to this Trial Chamber that we will respond in written form to this and confirming at the same time that we will need the seven and the 14 days. So it's not a request from my side. It is more information expressed towards the Court. And when I mean using 14 days, then I mean of course also for the Prosecution it's very important to file any earlier than possible. When we make, however, the assessment, we know what it is and what it means to implement a -- an operation to check and check out all the ramifications that comes out of allegations or a -- policy matters or any issues raised in the filing. We want to do that not quickly like assuming something or speculation or stating, we want to do a full response. So what my information towards your Trial Chamber is that we indeed tried to be as early as possible. We can aim for, let's say, Monday, but we cannot exclude that we will need more time, and that's only because we have to check things out and to address issues that aren't even easy to check in -- from an administration point of view. That's due to the fact -- to the very fact that we have disclosure issues, and it's always very difficult to address when it comes to earlier times years ago. Your Honour, with a view to the 92 bis application, that was only the opposing of one 92 bis witness. There are two announced and those two we don't know anything about it. But we also are very much aware of the fact that it's rather 92 bis than direct. But again, we will argue that from that position. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, it's just to underline that there's one 92 bis application done, and we will oppose that; and the other one we will wait for the proper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, the other one we are still waiting for. But the thing is this, Mr. Wubben. Almost a month ago now when this new accusation of non-disclosure of -- fresh violation of Rule 68 arose, we told you, Mr. Wubben, you're being told, it's being alleged, that notwithstanding your previous declarations of having fulfilled all your obligations under Rule 68, you're being told that you've still got some more skeletons in your cupboards, in your wardrobes. And we told you, Go and check your wardrobes, your cabinets, check every nook and corner to make sure that you haven't got any skeletons there. And you have come back telling us, We have done everything that we could. We don't have any more skeletons left. Then the Defence comes up and says, Well, that's not correct. There is a fresh allegation and promise of more to come, as I suspected all along. The question is -- I can't accept your arguments that you need much more time to do all these verifications. You are supposed to have done all these verifications. I can assure you, this is not going to change. This is not going to change. This is the tragedy of this case. This is not going to change. We will deal with this new allegation and we will hand down a provision, if it's necessary, and immediately after we'll have another one. This is how it's going to be. So at the end of the day, if you need until Monday, I'm prepared to give you until Monday. But please, don't put us in a worse position than we already are. We have an obligation to see this case through, and all these issues that are arising from time to time are only cutting down from the time we need to hear and finish with the evidentiary stage. I mean, we've lost almost half an hour already on this. So please try to come back with your response on the second one by Thursday, as that's the full seven days, and the other one by not later than Monday, Monday, the 28th, it will be, end of business on Monday, the 28th, which is not much less than the 14 -- than what the 14 days would have been. The 14 days would have been the 1st or 2nd of December, so we are not far off. That's it. And, please, do your utmost to put the mind of the Trial Chamber at rest that this business of alleged non-disclosure of -- under Rule 68, this will be the last time that we will be discussing or that we will have to discuss this in the courtroom. And that, in other words, there will not be any future need or any need for future discussions on further allegations on alleged Rule 68 violations. Because that is compromising the work of this Trial Chamber in that we are never in a position to plan correctly ahead. And already I've made my calculations. We've practically moved the evidentiary stage practically to the end of February, and this is not what I had in mind. This is the big problem. So I think I have dealt with that. The other -- the response that you have filed, Nikolic, I was not aware of it at all until a few minutes before I came into the courtroom. But, Mr. Pittman informed me -- he was not aware of it either, but I think he was made aware of it sometime before the sitting and I have a copy of it. So I will ask my two colleagues to -- they are in my exact, same, position. We were advised of its existence only a few minutes before. We will deal with it immediately. Immediately. And I thank you for the detailed response that you -- that you filed. I mean, it's a very good response. Any other -- are there any other preliminaries you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The other thing I wanted to know is this expert, finger-print expert -- not finger-print, sorry, the calligraphic expert. I am told you require five full days for his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will endeavour to make it as short as possible, but the thing is that he will have to give his expert opinion on at least 30 different documents. And if my -- in my assessment I can make it in a shorter time, you can rest assured that I will do so. But at this moment, I cannot tell you whether I'll be able to do it in a shorter period. Nonetheless, if I realise that it is possible in a shorter time, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The other thing is I would take it -- I mean, I am taking it for granted that he is going to file a written report, expert report. And basically, I mean my experience in trials is that he will supplement some information on the report, explain some parts maybe, but not go through each and every document unless he is led by you, and of course you have every right to go through each and every document. But the basis of his expert report will lie in the report itself, and then of course it's -- but five days. You meant five days for the Defence alone and not -- you're not including the cross-examination in those five days?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour. This includes both in chief and cross-examination. And there is a proposal for the other witness for two days. We also encompassed cross-examination in it. For Mr. Bilic, we foresaw six hours for testimony, and this is -- we also took the OTP into our calculations. But to reiterate, if we realise we can make that period shorter, we will endeavour to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Now some housekeeping announcements. Since the Milosevic trial will not be sitting this -- rest of this week, we have done the following arrangements. Tomorrow we are sitting in the morning in any case, Wednesday. Thursday we were sitting in the afternoon but now we are sitting in the morning, and Friday we are sitting in the morning, aren't we? I just want to confirm this because -- all right. Then the following week I think there is also -- this is December. There is also the 30th, the 30th, we are sitting -- we have swapped with the -- with Trial Chamber III, with the Milosevic trial, we will be sitting in the morning and not in the afternoon on the 30th. But on the 29th, we will be sitting in the afternoon. On the 29th, we will be sitting in the afternoon because I have Rules Committee in the morning, which was very difficult to fix in any case, and can only be done on that day. So there is no point in switching. The other thing that I wanted to say is that in all probability on Tuesday, 6th December, this I can check, 6th December -- yes, it might not affect our trial. We are going to have an extraordinary plenary, the Judges I mean, not you -- we are going to have an extraordinary plenary on the 6th. I take it that it will be in the morning, so it should not be impossible for us to meet with our commitments for an afternoon sitting at 2.15. But if there are any changes there, I would alert you -- alert you beforehand. All right. But do keep in mind that. So there is no point in trying to switch that sitting to the morning because we will be occupied in plenary on that day. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position is this: That if the 30th -- the sitting of the 30th is not switched to the morning, we will have to cancel it. That's definite. All right. So no more remarks or preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we need, members of the public, please -- we will need to bring down the curtains for a while until the witness walks in the courtroom. This witness is -- enjoys certain protective measures. You will be able to follow the proceedings, but you can't see this person walking in. As soon as he is seated, we will pull the curtains up again. He is going to be D005, isn't he? Facial and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, it's important that everyone makes sure that when the witness is speaking, all other microphones are switched off, all right? So good afternoon to you, and welcome to this Tribunal. Please wait --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait until I finish before you speak because I want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, it's important that everyone makes sure that when the witness is speaking, all other microphones are switched off, all right? So good afternoon to you, and welcome to this Tribunal. Please wait --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait until I finish before you speak because I want to make sure that it's only -- when you speak only your microphone is switched on. You are about to start giving evidence in this trial. Upon your own request, I, together with Judge Brydensholt from Denmark and Judge Eser from Germany, granted you some protective measures. These consist in the following. During the proceedings you will not be referred to by your name or by any other indication that could identify you. Your face will not be shown in the transmissions of this case, and your voice will be distorted. In other words, when you are giving testimony, others will not hear your true voice but they will hear a distorted version of it. Your testimony, however, will be in open session. In other words, others will be able to follow what you are saying. However, at any time we need to go into private session because otherwise your identity would be revealed, then of course we will be in private session and what you say will remain inside these four walls. For example, when we start with your testimony, Madam Vidovic will be asking you your name, your surname, where you were -- when you were born, where you live, and so on and so forth. If -- that information will not be in public session, it will be in private session, so that no one else will be able to hear what you are saying. Are you happy with these arrangements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Before you start giving evidence, our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath, in the sense that during the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper that is going to be handed to you by Madam Registrar. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us, that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Please take a seat. We can draw up the curtains. Now, sir, let me explain a few more things. I told you you will not be referred to by your name or your surname or anything else that could identify you, but we have given you a number. For the purposes of these proceedings, you are going to be D005, D005. And you will be addressed as "sir" or as "witness" as we go along. Try, while you are giving evidence, not to mention the names of any relatives of yours or the names of neighbours of yours as being neighbours, because at that point in time one could identify you. We still have a remedy that transmissions are delayed by 30 minutes, so if mistakes are made we have ample time to apply a remedy. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic will go first, as -- since you are a Defence witness, and she will then be followed by Ms. Sellers from the Prosecution team who will cross-examine you. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the first couple of questions I would kindly ask us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance in showing the witness a map, an excerpt from the topographical map of Zvornik. 1:100.000 is the scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please point to Konjevic Polje and mark it off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really find my bearings on many map. If it could perhaps be focussed a bit. Konjevic Polje should be over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the map and not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I was unable to see it because it was in the corner, Konjevic Polje, but I can see it here in this part of the map. So perhaps if this map could be placed ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give a pen or a marker to the witness so he can mark it off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it well now. Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Konjevic Polje a local commune before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show the Trial Chamber on this map the villages making part of the local commune of Konjevic Polje, if you can see all of them on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Racici, Borkovici, Pobudje, Konjevici, with all of their respective hamlets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the war, what was the ethnic make-up of the population of Konjevic Polje and its villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Konjevic Polje there were 5.500 Muslims and two households, or rather, two families who were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please show the Trial Chamber where Urkovici is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Urkovici, did it have its hamlets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Urkovici had four hamlets: Pervani, Sandici, Lolici, and Grabovsko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the names of the hamlets so that they could be correctly entered into the record. Witness, would you also please make a pause and wait for me to finish with my question and then speak more slowly so that everything could be entered into the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hamlets are Pervani, Grabovsko --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I make a technical intervention. If the map could be moved up so we could see where the witness is marking. I understand that this might be a little difficult. That way we can actually follow the evidence as given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I thank you, Ms. Sellers. Certainly that will be done. And also at the moment I'm a little bit preoccupied to make sure -- I'm following three screens, actually. The one on computer monitor to see where he is marking; secondly, since he is moving, going next to the ELMO, to make sure that his face and figure remain distorted, and we are having shots of the entire courtroom, and I'm making sure that he doesn't show up in any of them. So please bear with me. I assure you it's not an easy job, but that's what I have been trying to do. The map needs move, be centralised, which I think has been done now. Yes, let's continue now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the Prosecutor was speaking, I didn't hear you mention or mark off the villages of the hamlets of Pervani, Grabovsko, Lolici, Sandici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't managed to show them all. I can perhaps show them on the screen because I can see them more clearly here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, it has to be marked on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pervani is the hamlet of Urkovici, Grabovsko, Sandici, and Lolici, four villages in all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show Kravica to the Trial Chamber and perhaps use a marker of a different colour. Witness, I can't see that you have marked the villages. Could you please highlight them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These four villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please mark Kravica now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Sandici, the hamlet of Urkovici, far from Kravica -- far away from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what did the Muslim population living around Kravica -- what sort of experience did it have in World War II with the inhabitants of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During World War II the Kravica inhabitants, most of them were members of the Chetnik army so that the people living in my own village was -- were killed. I don't know if I can give you the name of the person who was in that previous war nailed to a tree. His limbs were nailed to a tree, and he was left standing there like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I will put to you another question in connection with this. Were some people from Kravica tried for war crimes after the World War II for the war crimes committed against the Muslims in the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Gojo Eric and his brother Nego Eric slaughtered some 86 persons in the village Sopotnik and Sedici [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they face a trial for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were sentenced to death; however, there was a retrial and they were given a sentence of some 18 years or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During Tito's Yugoslavia, were Muslims well-received in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as Kravica is concerned, Muslims were never welcome in Kravica, not even when they lived a peaceful life there. The people in Kravica were of such a peculiar character that they would not hesitate to even kill a person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Milosevic came to power, which Serb village in the Bratunac area, if any, spearheaded the nationalist movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Kravica itself. I know that they had a meeting at which Mile Milanovic was elected president of the SDS. At the time, wherever you came in Kravica, whether it was a shop or a cafe or a Serb house, you could see Milosevic's pictures everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned this particular meeting or session, and it wasn't unusual for such a meeting to be held. Can you tell us what sort of an atmosphere prevailed at this SDS meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to shots fired, which would happen even several days ahead of the meeting. However, when the meeting elected the SDS leadership one could hear shots even in the neighbouring villages, Obackici, Siljkovici, Banjevici, Brana and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything happening in September 1991 which caused particular concern to the population in the neighbouring area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the time it was primarily volunteers from Kravica who went to join the war against the Catholics in Croatia. They'd stayed there for five days and then come back at the weekend, come back to Kravica, where they would be shooting quite a lot, provoking people, wearing their cockade caps, Chetnik caps. They would be shouting out to the effect that similar things would be happening to us as well, that they would first kill that particular ethnic group and then would start killing us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall in the course of September 1991 that some murders were committed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well. It was about midnight that four young lads were passing by in a Lada car. They were going through Kravica in the direction of Bratunac. The Serb police pulled them over, because it was normally the Serb police who were on duty in Kravica. These boys knew that they were going to have problems with the police so they went to Bratunac. And in the hamlet of Kajici there was an ambush waiting for them there. And in the ambush there were Raso -- there was, among others, Raso Milanovic, and they killed two of the boys and two of them managed to run away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it able for you to know that Raso Milanovic was the perpetrator of these murders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know about this because the following day I went with a member of the reserve police force over there to see what had happened because I did not dare to go on my own. As we reached the spot, we found the two young men who had been killed and had been thrown into a pool of water there. And then I managed to pull the two men out on to a meadow. We thought that we were going to be able to find something on them, that they had been killed for some reason, like for self-interest, but they did not really have anything on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to add something else. Since this person with me was a member of the police reserve force, he inquired with his colleagues as to whether they knew who could have killed the two of them and told him that it must have been Raso Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we play a video, please. This is 2554. It is Prosecution Exhibit P448 from 1.19.01 to 1.19.053. Your Honours, we prepared the transcript of this excerpt, and I will distribute it before we play it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we play the excerpt now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] This place is of specific character, which is why it had a specific battle and survival in this war. The beginning of the war happened and we were simply exposed to all the ruthless events. Just before the war I was at the Croatian battlefield. I came to fight in this war, our war, simply as a patriot."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you recognise this person? Or rather, did you know him before the war, and if you did, who is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- it seems to be turned off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a problem, it seems, with interpretation. I forgot to tell you in the beginning if at any time the reception of the interpretation is faulty or else the level, sound level, is not agreeable to you, please draw our attention straight away and we will rectify the matter. Are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear the interpreters now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So it seems that if there was a problem it has been solved and we can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you if you used to know this man before the war, and if so, could you tell us who it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Raso Milanovic. I used to know him because he was Milo Milanovic's cousin, the SDS president in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this the person for whom you said that it was a well-known fact that he killed the two Muslims in Kajici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately, this is the person. And he was never brought to stand a trial in his entire life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, we -- because I take it that you would need -- you would be asking to have this transcript tendered into evidence and marked, given a number, but in addition, we haven't yet docketed the map. So the map that has been made use of with this witness until now and which was submitted by the Defence is being marked as Defence Exhibit D908. And the transcript from tape P448 is being marked D909.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the map be left with the witness, please, because we will need it during the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the witness, please, when he finishes with his testimony, be that today or whenever, in other words, when he is no longer going to refer to that map, I would like him to sign that map and that map will then go into the records and kept under seal. And that's because it will contain his name, so it will remain under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Related to the excerpt, I had another question. Did you know that Raso Milosevic -- I apologise, Raso Milanovic, was a volunteer at the Croatian battlefield?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that Raso Milanovic went to the Croatian battlefield as a volunteer, and he confirmed it himself, as we could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please kindly ask the usher to put another exhibit before the witness. This is D464.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, is it 464 or 646?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 646.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you get that, usher? Which document are you -- 646, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a dispatch by the security service centre Tuzla, state security service, dated the 13th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it a objection or what is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not in relationship to this document, and that's why I would like to put on the record before we move to the document. I've just had a chance to look at the transcript, and I see that Madam Vidovic's last series of questions was asking whether the witness knew that Raso Milanovic went to the Croatian battlefield as a volunteer. He says, yes, and he confirmed it himself. And I didn't know whether he was referring to a document that's now been marked Defence 909 or is this information that comes from a another place. I just wanted that clarified because I don't want to think that it comes from this transcript. Can we please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What doesn't -- I see your point. What doesn't come out of the transcript is the volunteer aspect of it. He does say in his interview that -- that that person, Milanovic, that he was at the Croatian battlefield, but that could mean that he was called, conscripted, in other words, and sent there or that he volunteered to go and fight in Croatia. So this is the point. You're assuming that he volunteered, but this does not really result from -- so this is -- is it important, Ms. Sellers, because at the end of the day he fought in Croatia and that's it. Whether he was called in response to a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect it might be important. It might be motivations in Croatia that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not question it. I just asked you whether -- because I don't know what you have in your mind in any case. Can we clarify this, Ms. Vidovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you know that Raso -- or whether Raso Milanovic was a volunteer before the war at the Croatian battlefield. Was this known in Kravica and its environs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When people went to the Croatian battlefields, all those who did were volunteers. Nobody left from Kravica mobilised. They all went of their own accord.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a look at the other document. Do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will quote the relevant part. It says: "Connection telephone conversation between Zoric Zdravko, head office, chief of the intelligence service and the minister of internal affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Drago Drakula, inspector of the second directorate of the state security service." This is a document dated the 13th of September, 1991, and -- thank you. "As a result of carrying out tasks from the plan of operations related to the murder of two persons of Muslim nationality in Konjic, municipality of Bratunac, dated the 3rd of September, 1991, four police officers of the Bratunac Open Security Service," and the names follow, were invited. And Cvjetinovic said that in the ambush next to Kobra was Radenko Milanovic, called Raso, from the municipality of Bratunac and that he was certain that he fired the shots at the vehicle during which the two Muslims were killed, whereas one person was likely wounded." My question pertaining to this, Witness, is the following: The contents of the document, does it tally with the information you mentioned you received from the person who attended the crime scene when the bodies were extracted from the body of water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is correct. And this tallies completely with what I heard and saw in Kajici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge, how many volunteers were there from the area of Kravica in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be specific as to the number, but certainly a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Muslims in the nearby villages scared of the events and everything that was taking place? Were they concerned with the fact that people from Kravica were leaving to Croatia to fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course they were scared and concerned. I was concerned as well, and I always thought I would be courageous enough not to experience such feelings. But if I felt that way, one can imagine what children and women felt like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who would return from the Croatian front, did they used to tell stories as to what was happening there in Croatia, stories of crimes perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they passed through our villages, they kept saying that they were killing and slaughtering and that they will slice our throats as well. They threatened us, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we could now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any movement of armed people as well as vehicles in the area of Kravica and its environs in 1992, that is, before the

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was at the beginning of 1992 and at the end of 1991 as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, Muslims of that area, have any knowledge as to any military training being conducted in your environs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs had a training ground or a school above the Bacici dam towards Banjevici. They had a training ground there and one could see that with the naked eye, one could see the soldiers, and shooting was heard all the time. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember when it was, the end of 1991 or beginning of 1992 or March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That was at the beginning of 1992 and further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that period, as of the beginning of 1992 onwards, you mentioned the shooting that you heard. Where did this shooting come from, what villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were quite a number of Serb villages around Kravica, and one could hear shooting from all of those villages, particularly during night. They didn't hide that. They were firing their weapons from their houses every evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the beginning of 1992, if you remember, could one freely move on the roads in the area or whether there were some barricades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992 one could move in Kravica but without stopping. We were prevented from stopping in the area of the local commune of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any barricades then in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The barricades were set up at the end of March next to Sveto's and Milo's houses in Kravica, as well as in Kajici towards the exit to Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During April and March of 1992, were you able to observe heavy weaponry in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and they didn't even try to hide it. At Siljkovici there was a Howitzer as well as an anti-aircraft gun. In Gornji Bacici there was a Howitzer. In Obackici there was a mortar and one could see it with the naked eye. And at Sveto's house there were three APCs and two tanks at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Vidovic. Let's go into private session for a minute. I just want --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned on several occasions Sveto's house. Is it at the very beginning of Kravica, at the very entrance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of Kravica, this is where Sveto's and Milo's houses are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Madam Vidovic. I'm informed that we require -- because of redactions, we require a 30-minute break and not 25. So we will have a 30-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, my following question has to do with the local population of Kravica. Did you notice in March and April 1992 that something was happening to the population there, namely women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of March and in early April, 1992, women and children were bussed over to Serbia, and the only ones remaining in Kravica were the able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you something in connection with Nego and Golub Eric, whom you have already mentioned as having been convicted for war crimes against Muslims. Did you know them well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them well. Once as I was on my way to Bratunac through Kravica I saw Golub Eric wearing a camouflage uniform and carrying a machine-gun. So he was -- this man was always there, regardless of his age, he was always a criminal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, I would ask that the witness not make conclusions about that, and it didn't seem to be in response to Madam Vidovic's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I said "I can imagine" because instead of answering his questions he jumped to conclusions, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you the following. As you saw these two men, did they have weapons on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Golub Eric had a weapon and a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance now in showing the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because it's not clear in my mind. In answering you -- the previous question -- in answering your previous question, he never mentioned that he saw them together on the same occasion. He said that he knew them well, and in fact at that point in time I was on my feet, almost, already to see -- in case he came up with some information that would reveal his identity. So I was on the lookout for that. But then he just mentioned that he saw that -- Golub Eric only. He never mentioned the other one as yet. So what I would like to know is whether on that occasion when he saw Golub Eric wearing a camouflage uniform and carrying a machine-gun he also saw the other one. And if he didn't, then he can perhaps explain to us how he knew these two persons well, because by seeing one of them wearing a camouflage uniform and walking down the street with a machine-gun doesn't mean that you know that person very well, particularly. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will be putting brief questions to you one by one. I have asked you whether you knew these two persons well, the ones that we mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew both of them well, but, as I've said, as far as Nego Eric was concerned he was an elderly man and wasn't moving about that often. However, Golub Eric, although an elderly man, was in good shape. I knew him very well because he would attend to some work in my village, therefore I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. This part that he attended to some work in his village, do you want it redacted or do you leave it there? It's up to you, Madam Vidovic, at this stage. I think -- I don't know, I don't want to interfere.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think there is need for that because he used to go to many villages to do some work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will ask you a different question now. Did you happen to see the two brothers together on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am of an advanced age myself. I am not that young, and I used to go to the centre of Kravica even before I went to school there. And of course I used to see them very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. My question was whether you saw them together in March or April 1992 -- or rather, when you saw them in March or April 1992, whether both of them were armed. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only Golub Eric was armed, and he wore a camouflage uniform. Nego Eric would not walk around with him because Nego Eric was his senior and they would move around in a car when they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the Defence Exhibit D45 to the witness. Your Honour, this is a document by the Bratunac Brigade containing a list of fallen fighters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please look at page starting with 115.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found it? I will quote under number 115 it is stated Eric, son of Mikailo Bogoljub, born 1914, killed on the 29th of May, 1992. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether Bogoljub Eric, son of Mikailo born in 1914, whether that was the same Golub Eric you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. His actual name is Bogoljub; his nickname is Golub. He got killed upon his return from Obackici when he was on his way to Urkovici. That was on the 29th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's near Kravica, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we move into private session for a while, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from the book entitled "Bloody Christmas in the Village of Kravica." Witness, I will read one section on page 42: "In mid-April a Crisis Staff was formed to which the following persons were appointed: Nedjo Nikolic, chairman; Krsto Cvjetinovic; Radomir, Raso, Milosevic; Bogoljub, Golub, Eric; Jovan Nikolic; Mile Milanovic; Dragan Ilic; Luka Bogdanovic; Slavisa Eric; and Nedeljko T. Nikolic. For safety reasons, the staff dismissed regular classes and turned the school building into a barracks. Special formations were organised." Witness, does this passage that I read out reflect what you saw in Kravica at the time when you went to talk to the person who you've mentioned? Was the school at this point actually a military facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that point the school must have been a military facility because on my way out of the new school building, because there was a new and an old school there, one could see soldiers in the old school carrying weapons and ammunition. These were people who were uniformed, and I do believe that the case was indeed as reflected here in this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the uniforms you saw like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were camouflage and olive-drab uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now go back to the names I read out. Did you know Nedjo Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's Djedura.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Raso Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was a driver in Vihor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already told us that you knew Bogoljub, Golub, Eric. Is that the person born in 1914?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also indicated that you knew Jovan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the headmaster of the school you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was the headmaster and a teacher in this elementary school in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mile Milanovic? Was that the person you mentioned as having been elected the president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the man. He's the son of Sveto Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the man you said was elected president of the SDS in Kravica on that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dragan Ilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was a police officer in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Luka Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He held a higher position compared to Dragan, and he was in Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "on a higher position," are you referring to a special institution? Where did he work? Special formation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he worked at the MUP. I don't know what his formation was, but he was on a position higher than Ilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that MUP in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Slavisa Eric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slavisa Eric was a nurse, and that's how I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he also from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. His house was next to the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now quote the second part of the book which was -- which is the last passage on page 42 which says -- can you please find the passage in order to follow. "The hearts of Kravica defenders were especially cheered up by the patriotic and voluntary arrival of active soldiers from the former JNA. Their assistance was necessary and their presence provided additional encouragement in the initial stage of the war. Some of them provided quality and precious military professional assistance, while others took part in organised collection of materiel and technical equipment. Lieutenant Colonel Djordje Nikolic largely contributed to this work." My question to you in connection with this is as follows: In the area of Konjevic Polje in April 1992, were you aware of the arrival of active-duty soldiers from the former JNA in the area of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've described this already. One could see it with the naked eye, although we also had binoculars from the vantage point where I was able to see everything, up from Sandici towards Kravica. One could observe that these were active-duty military personnel. One could observe this also from other vantage points with the naked eye because they did not really conceal their movements.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness a document by the command of the 363rd [as interpreted] Motorised Brigade dated 21st April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you continue, Ms. Vidovic, and before we finish with this document Judge Eser would like to put a question. Go ahead, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to point out that in this document, at least in the English translation, we do not have the full text, the first sentence, the hearts -- what was it called? I don't have it here now. Can you call it up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know what you mean, the hearts. I will go back myself. "The hearts of Kravica defenders were especially cheered up by the patriotic and voluntary arrival of active soldiers from the former JNA." That's page 42, last line, and 43, the first line. That's what you read, Ms. Vidovic. I mean, looking at the document I agree with Judge Eser, I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: It's not in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: However, there is something similar. "The patriotic and voluntary arrival of active soldiers from the former JNA, especially cheered up hearts and defenders of Kravica." I think that satisfies it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could the usher show the witness this particular document bearing the number 04343871. This is a document by the 336th Motorised Brigade dated 21st April, 1992. This is a brief document that I will quote. "To the command of the 17th Corps. Pursuant to your order, strictly confidential, 11/2-42, of 21st April, 1992, we wish to inform you that we have carried out the ordered resubordination. The following units have been incorporated into TG2. The 1st OKB, Armoured Battalion; the MSMC Mechanised Company of the 2nd OKB of the 453rd Mechanised Brigade; the Milici CTO; the Papraca CTO; one platoon of the Caparda CTO; and the Kravica JNA detachment. Commander Colonel Radovan Tacic." According to your knowledge, in April of 1992, did you notice the movement of soldiers and units of the JNA in the Kravica area and in the general Kravica area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I've already indicated that I noticed active-duty soldiers in the area of Kravica in Obackici, in Gornja Brana, Siljkovici. These are all the areas of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this document be assigned a Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document, Ms. Vidovic, is being given Defence exhibit -- becoming Defence exhibit D910 and it consists of two pages, one in B/C/S and one in English, with ERN 04343871. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a series of questions to put to you concerning the Muslims from Konjevic Polje. In April 1992, did the Muslims of Konjevic Polje, according to your knowledge, have any weapons? Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you can -- if you could put it that way, that we were armed, if having a hundred or so rifles means that we were armed. They were mostly hunting rifles and there may have been some automatic or semi-automatic weapons belonging to those who were members of the police. But there were very few as far as I know. Or if someone was able to buy rifles from Serbs. In total, there were about a hundred rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before the war, did some people start producing makeshift weapons at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Having realised what the preparations were about, we tried to produce rifles that would use hunting ammunition. However, we were not very good at that because the weapons that we produced were more dangerous for the one handling them than the target itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we move into private session now because I have some sensitive questions to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people you saw in Sandici and Urkovici, could one call that a village guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could not, not in any case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who came to ask of you to turn over your weapons, were they accompanied by APCs, tanks? Did they have machine-guns or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said that they all came there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood that you said that you were issued with an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an ultimatum. The weapons we handed over were insufficient for them. It seemed very little, of course, and they gave us the ultimatum that they will return in two days' time to collect the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's no longer quite as timely as it would have been a couple of seconds ago, but when the witness responded to Madam Vidovic's question regarding: Did they come with APCs and tanks? Did they have machine-guns or not? He said: "Yes, I said that they all came there," and that is not quite responsive. And I just would like to be clear because right now I don't know whether the tanks were there, did the people come in the tanks? And that was the question I was going to ask before we continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Sellers. My suspicion is that the witness answered before Ms. Vidovic had even finished her question; that's the problem. And I think you need to put the question again to the witness to make sure that he answers it because he did not answer your question. Thank you, Madam Vidovic. And thank you, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is probably an interpretation issue. I am unable to follow both during my examination-in-chief. I asked the witness not whether those people came in those APCs and tanks, but, rather I asked whether the APCs and tanks came as well, together with those people. That was the essence of my question. And the witness said: "Yes, I said that earlier." Witness, could you please clarify? Did I interpret your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you asked me previously I said that to Sandici APCs and tanks came, and there was another tank in Hrncici. Hence, the tanks (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You may proceed. I will sign the redaction form myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, based on the behaviour of Jole Nikolic as well as those other people in the APCs and the tanks, were you able to conclude whether they worked in unison or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They acted together, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said they issued an ultimatum. When did they return to Sandici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They returned, or rather, attacked Sandici and Urkovici on the 29th of May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe what was happening on the 29th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the early morning they attempted to use an APC to go through Sandici, Lolici, Pervani, and Hrncici to link up with Milici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did those people come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That APC and its personnel came from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the Muslim population of Sandici and Urkovici do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the APC was moving towards Konjevic Polje, we had a tree that we fell across the road. We thought someone might attack and we put it across -- so it had to slow down and people from the village could open fire at the APC. The personnel jumped out and ran back towards Kravica and the river, and they left the APC behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- was that the start of a fire or of a combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a relatively short combat. The APC was left behind and they ran away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only later when the APCs and tanks grouped at Milo Milanovic's house. That's when we saw tanks and APCs coming in as well as infantry, and I believe it was around noon that a fierce attack at Urkovici and Sandici was launched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the attack come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the direction of Kravica and its hamlets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the development of the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attack came from three APCs and tanks that came from Lolici and the infantry was standing next to the vehicles. The group from Obackici was headed by Golub Eric and he lost his life there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the elderly man born in 1914?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any victims on either of the sides on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, on both sides there were a number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serbs pull out their casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs pulled out those victims from Kravica, more or less, but they left behind the volunteers, people who came from elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you use those battles for? You filled them with gasoline and you put in corn peel and fuses. What did you use it for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had no other option in case of tanks coming through. We were at an elevation and this was our only way to defend. We wanted to throw those bottles at them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you tried to put those tanks on fire; did I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We had a truck that we put on the road as an obstacle and we wanted to set the truck on fire. The tanks try to come across. In any case, we wanted to prevent the APCs and the tanks to come through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The truck that was on fire, did it actually manage to stop the APCs and the tanks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They realised they couldn't get through and they tried to jump out of the APCs to take up positions with their infantry, and then the exchange of fire ensued and we received some help from Konjevic Polje and Hrncici. We had about 50 men who fought to prevent the tanks from coming in.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we put an exhibit before the witness. This is page 189 from the book entitled "Bloody Christmas."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will quote page 189 of the book. "The volunteers killed at the Kravica battlefield." Could you please look at numbers 3, 5, and 6. Miodrag Vorkapic killed on the 29th of May, 1992; Aleksandar Grahovac from Borovo Naselje killed on 29th May, 1992; Zarko Ivanovski from Prilep killed the 29th of May, 1992." I wanted to ask you the following: Were you able to see the bodies or the IDs of those killed on that day in Sandici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understood properly, those people from Borovo Selo were killed there. And we learned from their documents that they were killed from Croatia, that is, from the Serb Krajina in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, you saw their documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were brought by a neighbour of mine, if I may mention the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please don't. Most of those killed whose bodies were not pulled out, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Predominantly from the Serb Krajina in Croatia and from Serbia proper, that is, from Vojvodina, Novi Sad and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to put another document in front of the witness that is from the archive of the Drina Corps. It is entitled "list of persons who died in Sandici." Your Honours, could we please assign an exhibit number to this excerpt from the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. So this document which consists in the Serbo-Croat version of a photocopy of a drawing which seems to be the cover of the book and then two pages -- two pages, one of which is the first page of the book with the title, head, name of the author, and place and date of publishing. And in English three pages corresponding to the original text and being the translation thereof is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D911.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please take a look at this document, list of persons killed at Sandici. The number is 04544259 for the transcript. Please take a look at number 3. Milutin Milosevic, son of Stevo. Did you know this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war he was the chief of police in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in Urkovici or Sandici when the ultimatum for the surrendering of weapons was issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was in Sandici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take another look at this list. The first 11 people there were killed on the 29th of May in Sandici. Was Sandici a pure Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are all of these people Serbs, the people on this list of those killed? Were those the Serbs who attacked Sandici on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If one were to claim that on that day the Muslims from Sandici were actually attacking Kravica, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for another exhibit to be put before the witness. This is a Bratunac Brigade document dated the 26th of March, 1993, entitled "transport of bodily remains of fallen fighters," signed by Lieutenant Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, let's give this last document a number, Ms. Vidovic. This was document used with the witness which consists of two pages, one B/C/S, with ERN 04544259, and another page in English being the direct translation thereof with the same ERN number, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D912.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at the document where it says "transport of bodily remains of fallen fighters." I will quote: "Transport of bodily remains of fighters who were killed on 29 May 1992 in the village of Sandici at the territory of Bratunac Municipal Assembly is hereby approved." Further down, number 44: "Miodrag Vorkapic -- Novo Tenja." Underneath number 46: "Aleksandar" Grahovac -- Borovo Naselje." Could you tell the Trial Chamber where Novo Tenja and Borovo Naselje are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Novo Tenja and Borovo Naselje are to be found in the Serbian Krajina in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we assign an exhibit number to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Ms. Vidovic. And this document, which consists of two pages, both with ERN 04359358, one being in Serbo-Croat and the other one being the translation thereof into English, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D913.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance in showing the witness another new document. This is a document by the 1st Bratunac Brigade dated 24 March 1993, number 04359361. It's title is, again, "transport of bodily remains."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will quote this brief document to you. "On the 23rd of March, 1993, the identification of the bodily remains of the fighters who got killed on the 29th of May, 1992, in the village of Sandici, municipality of Bratunac, was carried out, namely, Vesna Krdzalic from Beli Manastir, Dragica Mastikosa from Novi Sad." And, Witness, could you tell the Trial Chamber where the towns of Beli Manastir and Novi Sad are situated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having been in Vojvodina quite often myself, I can tell you that both towns are in Vojvodina, Novi Sad being the capital of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are two fallen fighters on this list here who are women. Prior to these events in Sandici, did you learn anything about these women or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I learned about these women far earlier because there was stories about them having killed people in the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac and in Glogova because there was a man who came across the woods there and saw women killing people with knives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you? Where did these women commit these murders with knives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Glogova itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Azem present when these women got killed? Did he see their bodies in Sandici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He asked to be accompanied by his neighbour to go over there and see whether he could identify them. However, when he came down there and realised that these were in fact the two women that he had seen in Glogova, he was terribly frightened and even ran away from the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm clear when he says "was Azem present," was that something that was being suggested to the witness or if that refers to previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's a very legitimate question, Ms. Sellers. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I respond? The witness mentioned and probably -- I don't know if it entered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem as I see it, because I do recall having heard -- although I'm following the transcript in English, I do recall having heard the witness mention the name. So that's probably -- it's a problem of interpretation. But I would rather have the witness address this directly than you, Ms. Vidovic, to deal with it. What I want to know, sir, is how come you just decided to mention this Azem? Has the name been suggested to you by Madam Vidovic? Or had you mentioned the name before Madam Vidovic repeated the name? In other words, who informed you or who spread the rumours that these women had killed people in the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac? Who had told you about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told about this by Azem Rizvanovic because he was closer to Bratunac than I was and there was stories there about women killing people in Bratunac. And apparently the same thing happened in Glogova, and he was in the group where the two women were. He managed to escape the group and went across the woods in Ocenovici and reached Urkovici. I was there in Urkovici as he reached the place, and he was so afraid that he wanted all of us to run away from there. However, we convinced him to stay in Urkovici. He in fact stayed until the attack itself. After the attack, he asked to be allowed to go over there to take a look at the women to see if he could recognise them.
